Messages.Author: echia...@yahoo.com
Messages.Body:


While you may be right about the different attitude toward VTES in
Europe, I think your comparison may be off-base.

Yes, the U.S. has 300 million compared to Hungary's 10 million, but
you're also forgetting that the U.S. is over 100 times the size of
Hungary (about 9629091 km vs 93030 km). Factor the two together, and
you'll realize that Hungary has over three times the population
density as the U.S., which goes a long way towards explaining the
discrepancy in tournament size. (And yes, 10 sounds about right for a
U.S. tournament outside of the major cities). If you look at most of
the other European countries, you'll get similar results.

It's a distortion commonly mis-perceived by Americans with little
European experience and Europeans with little American experience. The
distance to get from one U.S. state to another neighboring U.S. state
is often equivalent or even greater than the distance to get from one
European country to its next door neighbor.

On Oct 9, 9:37 am, henrik <www.hen...@gmail.com> wrote:
> There was a smiley there, just for you.

The smiley was noted and factored in.

> I do think that there is some truth in it though. At least from what

> americans tend to look for the answer to losing in other things than

Well, no, not really. Like, certainly, I can only speak for myself,
but when I look for answers to things that I think make the game less
good than it could be, it isn't as the result of losing. It is the
result of seeing imbalance. I (or whoever) can use overpowered game
components just as much as anyone else can. I don't think Parity Shift
is too powerful 'cause I can't beat people who play Parity Shift. I
use Parity Shift all the time, and win with it all the time. And as a
result of using it and beating the crap out of people with it, my
assessment is "Parity Shift is probably too powerful" (along with
comparison and general cost/benefit analysis).

Banning RTI was not the result of "Wha! I keep getting killed by RTI
and can't figure out how to deal with it!" It was the result of "This
card is stupidly overpowered. Which is noted by playing it and
vaporizing people with it. And unless my prey is using bounce, they
get just outright killed. This card forces all decks to use bounce.
And makes the game, as a result, blow."

> If, when you lose a game, you blame the powerful cards your opponent
> played instead of looking at your own deck and play, you'll have a
> harder time evolving as a player.

And again, the issue is not "Waa! I can't beat X! It is clearly
broken!". The issue is "Huh. When I use X, it seems incredibly
overpowered. I wonder if other people have the same experience?"

The issue with contesting, similarly is not "Waa! I always lose when I
get contested! I don't know what to do about it!" it is "Huh. This
makes the game suck for everyone. And the game would probably be
better if it were fixed."

Assuming that people argue for things to be fixed 'cause they "can't
figure out how to beat them" is completely misunderstanding what is
going on here.

> It's a huge generalisation to say
> that all americans are this way and all europeans are that way, but
> the indications I've gotten from newsgroup discussions points me to
> that direction.

Then you are clearly misunderstanding the discussion.

-Peter

Messages.Author: Matthew T. Morgan
Messages.Body:
On Fri, 9 Oct 2009, Stefan Ferenci wrote:

> americans in general try to be more creative, less focused, while
> europeans in general play more agressive and are more concerned about
> winning than having a good time. just my two cents

Hey Stefan! Hope to see you in Palma (losing to me at the final table).

I think what you say may be true to a degree, but I think there's a reason
why. It isn't that Americans are more creative people or want to win
less. It's that we tend to have smaller playgroups and smaller
tournaments. When you attend a 10 player tournament, you can basically
play any deck that doesn't completely suck and you will have a 50% chance
of making the final. You can make the final by accident. You can make
the final with 1 VP sometimes. Good players know that any deck can win a
final by good seating choice, good luck, table dynamics, etc.

So Americans play a lot of "creative" (i.e. bad) decks. I know I do.
When you're instead looking at a 65 player tournament, you probably are
going to want to leave the Nagaraja vote deck at home if you want to make
the final because you're going to need a lot more than one lucky table to
get there.

If anything, I would say Americans maybe have some trouble adjusting to
the larger tournaments. We tend to still play our silly decks that do
okay at home because we don't play that many large tournaments or when we
do, we play against other Americans who are also playing silly decks.
Having played more than a few friendly games on your side of the Atlantic,
I know that Euros do build and enjoy the same stupid decks that Americans
do. They just don't bring them to major tournaments. I can recall you
playing some kind of Huitzilopotchtli Condemntation deck when I visited
Vienna.

Matt Morgan

Messages.Author: Aaron Clark
Messages.Body:
I agree with what Matt Morgan said. I think you can look at the First
Chance Qualifier final to see some truth in people's comments. There
were four Americans and one European, Erol, who won. I personally was
playing a silly deck that I qualified with essentially through luck.
It was a Cassandra, Magus Prime superstar deck using Celerity &
Thaumaturgy hand strikes, smaller Dominate vampires for support, and
some Tremere toolbox stuff. With luck and Dominate, the deck has
gotten me to two finals, but I know it's probably not going to win a
tournament. It's just fun to play. The other Americans were playing
very good decks, but I'm not sure how their deck archetypes stacked up
in the scale of Tier 1, 2, etc. (weenie Auspex w/combat allies,
Animalism/Deep Song featuring Ashur Tablets, Toreador vote with new
tech).

Erol, the European winner, was definitely playing a Tier 1 deck:
Ventrue/Vote/Obfuscate/Mind Rape starring Arika. His deck had 8 Mind
Rapes, which would set you back $200+ on E-bay right now. He is also
an amazing player, somehow getting other players to do things (like
rescuing Arika from torpor) that they really shouldn't do and just
playing very well.

When I saw his deck in Game 2, I knew it outclassed everything else on
the table, and I think it also outclassed everything at the final
table. It was a killer deck.

In my local playgroup, I think there has been a shift from scarily
competitive decks when I started playing again last year to decks that
are creative yet still competitive. It's more fun, but you don't have
to have a killer deck every time to keep from being ousted in the
first 30 minutes. When we have tournaments or a lot of visiting
players, the competition intensifies, but that only happens a few
times a year.

If those other play groups were closer or there were more tournaments
here, I think all my decks would have to be much more tuned to keep
up. Europeans are going to be more competitive just because they can
be in more tournaments and travel to more play groups.

Well, population density helps explain some of it, but you can break
down the issue even more:

- To improve accuracy, you also need to look at where the population
centers are within the particular country. For example, Russia,
Canada, and Denmark (if you consider Greenland but most calculations
don't seem to include it) contain vast stretches of unoccupied land -
their populations are significantly concentrated in certain locations,
so using a straightforward population density metric may be
misleading.

- Also, the shape of the land is also relevant. Chile is roughly the
same size as Turkey, but transportation in Chile is going to be much
more challenging if you live on one end of the country and are trying
to get all the way across to the other. This problem is evident in the
U.S. if you look at the East Coast compared to the West Coast -
distance between these playgroups is a significant barrier.

- And of course, there may also be cultural factors (religiosity may
affect the popularity of a game about vampires), economic factors
(prevalence of gaming stores), and demographic factors (populations
with lots of minors or lots of senior citizens are less likely to have
lots of VTES players). Etc.

One thing I am impressed by my fellow Americans, is a greater
willingness to travel for casual/local tournaments. It's quite normal
to travel an hour away to get to a nearby tournament, and driving 2-3
hours or more is not unheard of either. In contrast, from what I've
heard many Europeans are loathe to travel to neighboring countries for
events even if the physical distance may not be too significant
(exception for major tournaments/qualifiers/championships).

Two final anecdotes which might provide some additional perspective.
While living in the U.K. I was pleasantly surprised to learn that many
letters and packages arrive within a day (sometimes two) of sending
them. In the U.S., you'd regularly expect up to 3-5 days, so it was
nice to receive an order the very next day. Similarly, some of the
Brits were often surprised when I mentioned that I lived in the
Chicago suburbs, an hour away from the city. They'd often reply that
if they lived an hour away from London, they wouldn't consider
themselves to be from London! But what explains these phenomena is
that England (which constitutes a little over half the land area of
the United Kingdom), is actually a bit smaller than the state of
Illinois. So if your comparison is mailing within the state (instead
of across the country), you have a better idea of the geographic
context. Not to mention that England has 51 million people compared to
Illinois' 13 million - making it four times as dense.

Getting back to the Hungary example, Hungary is just slightly smaller
than the state of Indiana. Hungary has about one and a half times the
population of Indiana. Budapest has twice the population of
Indianapolis, but only half as large in land area, resulting in a
population density four times as large. In Indiana, you also have some
split population centers. Besides the hub in central Indiana
(Indianapolis), you also have significant pockets in the Northwest
(around Gary, which are more affiliated to Chicago/Illinois than to
Indianapolis) and in the North/Northeast (which probably have closer
ties to Michigan/Ohio). I'm not an expert on Hungary, but I'd hazard a
guess that the population in Indiana is probably more fractured than
that of Hungary (which benefits from national sentiment). So in
conclusion, trying to compare Hungary to the entirety of the United
States, is going to lead to a distorted perspective.

And this seems like a solid enough explanation to the why. We've had
the same problem in Sweden from time to time and at those times we
(the players that are good enough and interested enough to be
bothered) has to look outside our borders to learn more about VtES. So
we looked to Germany, Hungary, Switzerland, and of course we looked to
France and we learned alot. Guess we looked all over the world with a
focus on France.

We do however still have the benefit of these big VtES countries being
rather close to us. As an example it usually costs about 100 SEK for
the flight and 250 SEK for the bus to go to the nationals in Germany
from Göteborg where I'm located. If you're located in Örebro or
Stockholm you can make the same trip to both Germany or France.

My point is that in those times where we suffer reduced numbers of
players in the Swedish tournaments we are still pretty close to the
rest of Europe and have every opportunity to join the discussion and
play in the big events. I would imagine that it is harder to do this
if you're, like you, located on the US east coast.

Regards
Alex

> drawing that many players. Freaking Hungary - 10.5million people,
> compared to 300+million Americans.

Agreed - Hungarians just kick ass! :)

But yeah, beside that, there are other factors (as more or less
mentioned elsewhere). The main point is, however, that V:tES is
popular in Hungary because there are a number of influential
V:tES players (e.g. store owners) who promote the game.

Another point not mentioned is that the Hungarian National
Championship is organised for the 4th year in a row to bring
high-level tournaments close to the players living in the
smaller cities.

There are also special newbie tournaments, where the prizes are
low, but each entrant gets a truckload of useful commons /
vampires, plus each table gets a judge who offers advice after
each game.

I think more than anything, enthusiastic people (especially store
owners) make or break the V:tES community. The rest is mostly
logistics.

For the sake of completeness, I must mention that V:tES was stronger
in Hungary about 5-6 years ago - we had 60-80 people tournaments,
compared to the current 40s. There are a number of factors (old
timers getting kids, some people leaving the game, folks skipping
the "unfun" tournaments, organiser focus on 40-something tournaments)
causing this.

--
Regards,

Daneel

On Oct 9, 6:51 pm, Martel732 <bowle...@gmail.com> wrote:

> I haven't played in a couple of years, but I plan on getting back to
> it next year. I really would have to get back into the game to discern
> all these tiers of decks, but in Cincinnati we have seen a lot of
> combat-heavy play that seems to do well against Euro-style decks.
> Arika can't do much in torpor. Any other Ohio players want to chime
> in?

Not an Ohio player, but one factor that may affect what you observe is
the density of combat on the table. If there are 3 combat decks, and
1 or two squishy decks, those "fast, tier 1" decks tend to get
clocked. And then the combat decks can either coin flip for the win,
because combat vs. combat is the most random element of play, or the
person who manipulates the table best wins. Flip it around, though,
and be the lone combat deck on a table full of fast non-combat, and
you're probably a king maker.

--

David Cherryholmes

One of the weird things is how East Asia factors into the density
discussion. VtES Japan is all but an unknown quantity -- there, but
not much correspondence. And VtES Korea is non-existent (I know, I
looked. Couldn't find anything. D: ). However, if you look at their
land and city density levels, they blow Europe out of the water. And
they do have gamers galore, both PC and table, so that's not really
the problem.

Part of the issue might be the ideas of public spaces. There's a place
every few feet to drink coffee or alcohol in Tokyo or Seoul, but
rarely do you see regulars sitting at the bar shootin' the shit
(unless it's an expat place). Often drinking culture is communal, as
in you go to a location together as a group, and bar hop as a party.
It's not like meeting regulars or friends at a designated watering
hole and passing the time. And further these get-togethers are
business oriented or date oriented, precluding VtES being the
prominent form of entertainment.

Also people do not play as openly at school campuses or libraries and
the like -- well from what I've seen. Usually, if I saw anything, it
was at Game Rooms where they rent time and table space to play games.
They work essentially like PC cafes with food and drinks available and
service to bring it to you if you were busy. And most of these places
tended to be dating places, where couples could play Settlers of Catan
or Uno, wear silly hats, and hit each other with squeaky toy hammers.
I don't know if that is conducive recruiting territory (at least, I
never tried to introduce VtES here).

So, I think there is definitely something else involved with why
Europe likes VtES so much. Perhaps it has to do with density AND a
cultural framework of how to use public space and socialize with
friends?

Well, that can be said about all levels and types of hobby gaming (CCGs,
RPGs, and Miniature games (all tabletop)).

I think it's because a) there hasn't been a set that specifically
addresses Asia. MTG had the 3 Kingdoms set (which may have come after
it was popular in Japan/China/Korea). And b) no marketing done in
Japan. If WW/CCP partnered with the right stores, they could have some
presence.

Another thing that specifically relates to Japan, and maybe the other
countries. Japanese tend to be very brand conscious. MTG, Pokemon, YGO
are very strong brands. VTES, not so much. For that reason I think the
VTES hasn't taken more than a toehold there.
